html:
1How to use this recap, and the exam map

How to Use This Recap

  • Nothing new: every page repeats what modules 1 to 13 taught, in a form you can scan
  • Cover and recall: hide the right-hand side of a table, answer from memory, then check
  • Follow the module tags: each page names where the detail lives, so you can go back
  • Mind the tags: pages marked Dates or Verify live hold facts that change, so confirm them before the exam
  • Numbers and dates are as of the dated line on each tagged page
  • Use it to find gaps, not to replace the modules

The Exam Map: Four Domains, Thirteen Competencies

  • Domain I (16 to 20 questions): foundations, harms and principles, roles and training, policies
  • Domain II (19 to 23): privacy laws, other existing laws, AI-specific laws, standards and frameworks
  • Domain III (21 to 25): the use case, design, data, testing and release, monitoring and incidents
  • Domain IV (21 to 25): context, models and options, assessing the system, governing use
  • The ranges show weight, not a promise

Exam tip: Every question counts the same, so spread your last revision across all four domains.

2Roles, risk tiers and duties

Roles by Law

  • AI Act roles follow the system: provider, deployer, importer, distributor, authorized representative
  • GDPR roles follow the personal data: controller, processor, and joint controllers (GDPR Article 26)
  • One organization can hold several roles: Helios is a deployer of the hiring tool and a provider of the assistant built on a model it uses
  • Roles can change: putting your name on a high-risk system, or modifying it substantially, makes a deployer a provider (Article 25)
  • Processors work under a contract with set terms (GDPR Article 28)

Exam tip: Identify the role first: the duties follow the role, not the size of the company.

EU AI Act Risk Tiers and What Each Brings

  • Prohibited (Article 5): manipulation, exploiting vulnerabilities, social scoring, crime prediction by profiling, face-scraping, workplace and school emotion inference, and more
  • High-risk (Article 6): Annex III areas, such as employment, and safety components under Annex I
  • Transparency (Article 50): people told they are interacting with AI; synthetic content marked
  • Minimal risk: no specific duties; voluntary codes
  • General-purpose models (Articles 51, 53, 55): documentation, copyright policy and training summary; extra duties for systemic risk

Exam tip: Classify the system by its use, then read off the duties for that tier and for your role.

Provider and Deployer Duties Side by Side

  • Provider: requirements (Articles 9 to 15), quality management (Article 17), conformity steps (Articles 43, 47, 48, 49)
  • Provider in use: instructions for use (Article 13), post-market monitoring (Article 72), serious incident reporting (Article 73)
  • Deployer (Article 26): follow the instructions, assign competent oversight, check input data, monitor, keep logs for at least six months
  • Deployer, where it applies: fundamental rights impact assessment (Article 27)
  • Both: transparency duties (Article 50)

Exam tip: The provider proves the product; the deployer governs the use.

3Penalties and timelines

Penalties Compared

  • AI Act, Article 99: prohibited practices up to EUR 35 million or 7%; most other obligations up to EUR 15 million or 3%; incorrect or misleading information up to EUR 7.5 million or 1%
  • Whichever is higher applies, but for small and medium-sized enterprises and start-ups the lower applies
  • General-purpose model providers: the Commission may fine up to 3% or EUR 15 million (Article 101)
  • GDPR, Article 83(5): up to EUR 20 million or 4% for breaches of the basic principles, data subject rights and transfer rules
  • Both regimes can apply to the same facts

Exam tip: The AI Act's top tier is higher than the GDPR's, and it is reserved for prohibited practices.

Timelines at a Glance [Dates] [Verify live]

  • 2 February 2025: the first prohibitions and the AI literacy duty
  • 2 August 2025: general-purpose model rules, governance and penalties
  • 2 August 2026: the Act applies generally; 2 December 2026: new prohibitions
  • 2 December 2027: Annex III high-risk systems; 2 August 2028: Annex I high-risk systems
  • 9 December 2026: the Product Liability Directive applies to products placed on the market from then
  • As of 27 October 2026: dates were moved by the Digital Omnibus on AI; confirm them before the exam

Exam tip: Know the order of the milestones and what each starts, not just the dates.

4Comparing the instruments

Privacy Law and AI Law Compared

  • GDPR: protects people's personal data and rights; applies to any processing of personal data, with or without AI
  • AI Act: regulates AI systems by risk; applies to systems placed on the Union market or whose output is used there
  • Tools differ: GDPR uses lawful basis, principles, rights and the DPIA (Article 35); the AI Act uses tiers, requirements and conformity
  • They overlap: an AI system that processes personal data is under both; the fundamental rights impact assessment (Article 27) may cross-refer to a DPIA
  • Other laws add more: consumer protection, nondiscrimination, product liability and sector rules (module 5)

Exam tip: When a case involves personal data and AI, check both laws before choosing an answer.

NIST, ISO and OECD Compared

  • NIST AI RMF 1.0: voluntary; four functions, Govern, Map, Measure, Manage; 19 categories and 72 subcategories; profiles and a Playbook
  • ISO/IEC 42001: a management system standard; clauses 4 to 10; Annex A with 38 controls in nine objectives; certifiable
  • OECD AI Principles: non-binding; five values-based principles and recommendations for policy makers
  • Together at Helios: ISO to structure the program, NIST to run risk per system, the EU AI Act as the legal floor, the OECD principles as the basis of policy
  • ISO/IEC 42005 gives guidance on impact assessment (module 7, depth marked)

Exam tip: Voluntary framework, certifiable standard, non-binding principles: match each to its nature.

5The life cycle and the reporting clocks

The Life Cycle and Where Each Control Sits

  • Plan and design (module 8): use-case approval, impact assessment, human oversight design, metrics
  • Data and build (module 9): data governance, lineage, testing, fairness metrics, model card
  • Release (module 10): readiness gate, conformity, staged release, rollback
  • Deploy (modules 11 to 13): context, model and option, assessment of the chosen system, contract, training, oversight
  • Monitor, maintain, retire (modules 10 and 13): monitoring, drift, periodic checks, incidents, deactivation

Exam tip: For any scenario, find the life-cycle stage first, then pick the control that belongs to it.

Reporting Clocks at a Glance

  • AI Act, Article 73: serious incidents are reported not later than 15 days after awareness, 2 days for a widespread infringement and 10 days after a death
  • GDPR, Article 33: a personal data breach is notified without undue delay, where feasible within 72 hours
  • A processor tells the controller without undue delay (Article 33)
  • A deployer informs the provider and suspends use where there is a risk (Article 26)
  • Contracts may set shorter notices, and one event can start several clocks

Exam tip: One event can start several clocks, and the shortest applicable one governs.

6Glossary

Glossary 1: Concepts and Risks

Term Meaning Term Meaning
AI system Machine-based system that infers how to generate outputs Generative AI Creates new text, images, code or audio
Predictive model Scores, classifies or predicts General-purpose AI model Broad model used in many downstream systems
Confabulation Confident but false output Bias Systematic skew in data, model or use
Fairness Comparable outcomes for comparable people Impact ratio Selection rate of one group over another
Explainability Giving reasons for an output Transparency Openness about what a system is and does
Robustness Holding up under noise or attack Drift A shift in data or behavior over time
Overfitting Memorizing training data Data leakage Test data leaking into training
Automation bias Over-trusting the output Human oversight A person who can understand, override and stop
Red teaming Trying to make a system fail Prompt injection Hidden instructions that hijack a model
Model card Plain record of a model's use and limits Data lineage Traceable path of data from source to model

Glossary 2: Roles, Law and Assessment

Term Meaning Term Meaning
Provider Develops and places a system on the market Deployer Uses a system under its authority
Importer Brings a non-Union system to the market Distributor Passes a system along the supply chain
Controller Decides purposes and means of processing Processor Processes on the controller's behalf
DPIA Data protection impact assessment FRIA Fundamental rights impact assessment
High-risk system Annex I or Annex III system with full duties Prohibited practice A banned use under Article 5
Conformity assessment Check before market placement CE marking Sign that conformity was shown
Systemic risk Risk from the largest general-purpose models Serious incident Death, serious harm or major disruption
Instructions for use Provider's guide for deployers Technical documentation Provider's record of design and testing
Substantial modification Change needing a new assessment Post-market monitoring Provider's watch on a system in use

Glossary 3: Frameworks and Practice

Term Meaning Term Meaning
Govern, Map, Measure, Manage The four NIST functions Profile A NIST view of a use case, time or sector
Playbook NIST's suggested actions Statement of applicability ISO list of chosen controls
OECD principles Non-binding values for trustworthy AI Three lines Management, risk oversight, internal audit
Risk appetite Level of risk the organization accepts Risk register List of risks with owners and controls
Incident register Record of incidents and near misses Change control Test, approve, release, monitor
Kill switch Tested way to stop a system Fallback A manual or older process
Localize Limit a system by region or feature Indemnity Vendor's promise to defend and pay
Shadow AI AI used without registration Pre-mortem Imagine the failure, then work out why
Staged release Small share first, then wider Rollback Return to the previous version

7Which instrument applies?

Which Instrument Applies? A Decision Aid

  • Personal data? GDPR, with a DPIA where the risk is high
  • AI system on the EU market, or output used in the EU? the AI Act: classify the tier, then the role
  • Hiring in New York City? Local Law 144: bias audit and notice
  • Defective product causing harm? the Product Liability Directive
  • Management system, risk guidance or policy values? ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF, the OECD principles

Exam tip: Name the situation, the role and the life-cycle stage first; the instrument usually follows.
